extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers of social and cultural history of London fairs and popular amusements (17th–early 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the contemporary regulatory and customary standards governing entertainments, shows, and exhibitions at London fairs (Bartholomew, May, Southwark) around the late 17th and early 18th centuries. Focuses on licensing, prohibitions, enforcement, and commercial practices revealed in advertisements and official orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing of ballad-singers (office of the revels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ballad-singers were required to take out licenses at the office of the revels at Whitehall; licensing of ballad-singers had been rented/let by the Master of the Revels (Charles Killigrew) to a bookseller (John Clarke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Announcement (London Gazette, 1682) directs ballad-singers to 'take out licenses at the office of the revels, at Whitehall, for singing and selling of ballads and small books, according to an ancient custom.' The lease of licensing to John Clarke is noted; licensing appears to be a controlled, revenue-generating privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory license form and authentication for showmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Showmen (mountebanks, rope-dancers, prize-players, ballad-singers, and those who make shows of motions and strange sights) were required to have a license 'in red and black letters, under the hand and seal' of the Master of the Revels (Charles Killigrew, Esq.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The London Gazette notice (1682) warns to 'suppress all mountebanks, rope-dancers, prize-players, ballad-singers, and such as make show of motions and strange sights, that have not a license in red and black letters, under the hand and seal of the said Charles Killigrew, Esq., Master of the Revels to his Majesty.' This specifies formality of licensing and indicates active suppression of unlicensed performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of booths for interludes, stage-plays, comedies, gaming, lotteries, and music meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders from the Lord Mayor and Court of Aldermen (circa 1700) forbade erection or use of booths, sheds, stalls, or other erections for interludes, stage-plays, comedies, gaming-places, lotteries, or music meetings during the fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grand jury presentment (1701) quotes the printed order (25 June 1700) and repeats a similar order (3 June), thanking the Lord Mayor and urging vigorous prosecution. The text frames these entertainments as 'chiefest nurseries of vice next to the play-houses' and seeks to limit fairs to non-entertainment/market uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific ban on music-booths and any booths promoting debauchery
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensing granted for booths during Bartholomew Fair explicitly excluded music-booths and 'any that may be means to promote debauchery'; magistrates ordered immediate removal of music-booths when encountered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 1700 resolution granting limited licenses to erect some booths stated 'but none are permitted for music-booths, or any that may be means to promote debauchery.' On proclamation of the fair the Lord Mayor ordered two music-booths to be taken down immediately—showing both the substance of the prohibition and prompt enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-of-fair purpose standard (market vs. amusement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials and grand jurors asserted that Bartholomew Fair should be employed for the 'good ends and purposes it was at first designed' (annual market/merchandize) rather than as a locus of amusements deemed profane or debauching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grand jury's presentment laments 'the great profaneness, vice, and debauchery' at the fair and urges that orders be 'vigorously prosecuted' so the fair 'may be employed to those good ends and purposes it was at first designed.' This sets an evaluative standard for acceptable activities (commerce/market) versus forbidden entertainments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement expectation: vigorous prosecution and removal of offending booths
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities and the grand jury expected active enforcement—removal of prohibited booths and prosecution of offenders—to uphold orders limiting entertainment at the fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presentment 'earnestly desire[s] that the said orders may be vigorously prosecuted,' and contemporaneous actions (Lord Mayor ordering music-booths taken down; arrests and punishment for other disturbances) illustrate the enforcement mechanism and expectation of prompt action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial/exhibition practice standards (advertised hours, admission, and conveniences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements for exhibitions specified admission charges, opening hours, and facilities (e.g., 'exposed to view, for sixpence a piece', open from eight in the morning to eight at night; back-door 'for the conveniency of the Gentry').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a 'Monster' at Moncrieff's Coffee-house was 'exposed to view, for sixpence a piece' and shown from eight in the morning to eight at night; some booths advertised a back-door for the convenience of gentry—these commercial terms functioned as de facto standards of exhibition practice and audience management.
